lead: A search radar sweeps a volume and reports whatever it finds. A tracking radar stares at one target and follows it with a servo loop that keeps the antenna pointed. That loop needs an angle error signal: a voltage that is zero when the antenna points exactly at the target and changes sign when the target drifts off. Three classic methods build it: sequential lobing, conical scan, and monopulse. Monopulse gets the error from a single pulse, which is why airport approach radars and missile seekers use it.
prereq: You need 6.1 for the antenna and receiver chain, and Unit 3 for beam squint and array patterns.

sections.h3: From search to track: the error signal

blocks.text: A search radar sweeps its beam through a volume and reports every echo, with an angle only as fine as the beamwidth. A tracking radar picks one target and stays pointed at it. It closes a loop: antenna, receiver, angle error, servo motor, back to the antenna.

Boresight is the electrical axis of the antenna: the direction in which the angle error signal is zero. A little to one side the error takes one sign, a little to the other side the opposite sign, and its size grows with the angle. A clean zero crossing at boresight is the whole requirement.

blocks.where: ε is the angle error voltage in volts; θ is the off-boresight angle in degrees; k is the error slope in volts per degree, set by the beam shape — a narrow beam gives a steeper slope.

items: The antenna dwells on the predicted target position for one or more pulses.
The receiver measures the echo and the angle sensor produces ε.
The servo amplifies ε and turns the antenna until ε falls to zero.
The loop keeps the antenna in step with the target's motion.

blocks.text: The loop is a control system. Its bandwidth must be wide enough to follow a manoeuvring aircraft and narrow enough to average out receiver noise.

Sequential lobing, also called lobe switching, uses two beams squinted to either side of boresight and switches between them pulse by pulse. A target on boresight gives equal echoes; a target off to one side gives a bigger echo in the nearer beam, and the difference carries the angle.

blocks.where: A_L and A_R are the echo amplitudes on the left and right beams; ε is zero on boresight and changes sign across it; θ is the off-boresight angle and k absorbs the proportionality.

items: The beams are sampled on different pulses, so a target whose echo strength fluctuates looks like a moving target and produces angle noise.
Each beam gets only half the dwell time, which costs signal-to-noise ratio.
It is simple and needs one receiver, but it is slow.

blocks.text: Conical scan uses one beam, squinted off axis and rotated about the boresight at the scan rate — a few tens of hertz — so the beam traces a cone. The echo amplitude then rises and falls once per revolution. The depth of the modulation gives the size of the angle error; its phase, compared with the rotation, gives the direction.

items: One receiver and one feed, so it is cheap and was standard on early airborne and shipborne radars.
The scan-rate modulation is a known signature: a jammer that repeats the echo amplitude-modulated at the scan rate creates a false angle error and pulls the antenna off target.

The scan rate lies in the band where target fading and glint carry most of their energy, so a filter tuned to the scan rate cannot separate real angle modulation from amplitude noise. Doppler processing does not help either, because the scan-rate sidebands sit far below the target Doppler shift, which is in kilohertz and above.

sections.h3: Monopulse: sum and difference from one pulse

blocks.text: Monopulse means simultaneous lobing. Four horns, each squinted into one quadrant, feed a comparator built from magic tees or hybrid rings (see waveguide tees and directional couplers). The comparator adds and subtracts the four signals to form three channels.
Σ = A + B + C + D;  Δaz = (A + B) − (C + D);  Δel = (A + C) − (B + D)
blocks.where: A, B, C, D are the signals from the four squinted beams; Σ is the sum channel used for detection and range; Δaz and Δel are the difference channels, each zero when the target is on boresight in that plane. Number the horns A top-left, B bottom-left, C top-right, D bottom-right. Then A + B is the left column, C + D the right column, A + C the top row, B + D the bottom row.
θ is the angle error in degrees; Δ/Σ is the difference-to-sum ratio, a pure number; k is the error slope in per degree, measured in calibration.

blocks.text: Dividing by Σ is what makes the reading useful. A strong echo and a weak echo from the same direction give very different Δ but the same Δ/Σ, so the indicated angle does not depend on range, target size or transmitter power. Because all four beams are sampled by the same pulse, target fluctuation cannot create an angle error. The cost is hardware: three matched receivers, or one receiver switched fast between channels.

Phase-comparison monopulse uses two parallel beams from separate apertures instead of squinted beams. The angle comes from the phase difference between the received signals, needing phase detectors that share one reference oscillator. Only a few universities teach it in detail; the normalisation and the servo are the same.

sections.h3: Range tracking, memory and accuracy limits

blocks.text: Angle is half the job; the range gate must track too. A split gate places an early gate and a late gate either side of the echo. If the echo is centred, both collect equal energy; if it drifts, the difference drives the gate delay and the range reading follows.

items: Acquisition puts the target inside the gates and switches the loop to track; loss of echo puts the loop into memory, where it coasts on the last velocity until the target reappears.
Thermal noise sets a random angle error that falls as the error slope rises and as signal-to-noise ratio rises.
Glint is worse than noise: when two scattering points on an aircraft add and cancel, the apparent position wanders by metres.

figure.caption: Four squinted beams feed one comparator. The sum channel serves detection and range; each difference channel, divided by the sum and scaled by the slope, gives an angle error.

spec.aria: Monopulse comparator tree: four squinted beams are added to give the sum channel for detection and range, and subtracted pairwise to give azimuth and elevation difference channels whose ratio to the sum gives the angle error.

examples.question: A monopulse radar reads Δ = 1.2 V and Σ = 10 V on the same pulse, with error slope k = 1.8 per degree. (a) Find Δ/Σ. (b) Find the angle error. (c) Find the cross-range offset at range 20 km. (d) What does the servo do next?
steps: Δ/Σ = 1.2 V / 10 V = 0.12, a pure ratio.
The servo drives the antenna 0.0667° toward the target so that Δaz returns to zero.
examples.answer: Δ/Σ = 0.12, the angle error is 0.0667° (a cross-range offset of 23.27 m at 20 km), and the servo turns the antenna 0.0667° to null the difference channel.
examples.check:
import math
sigma = 10.0
delta = 1.2
k = 1.8
R = 20000.0
ratio = delta / sigma
theta = ratio / k
offset = R * math.tan(math.radians(theta))
print(round(ratio, 2))
print(round(theta, 4))
print(round(offset, 2))

traps: Using Δ alone as the error. Without dividing by Σ the indicated angle changes when echo strength, range or target size changes. The error signal is Δ/Σ.
Monopulse means one pulse, not one beam: it needs several squinted beams or apertures, a comparator, and parallel receiver channels.
In conical scan the modulation depth gives the size of the angle error and the phase gives the direction. Swapping these two inverts the correction.
The error slope k is in volts per degree in the lobing form and per degree in the ratio form. Mixing degrees and radians throws the answer off by 57.3.
Sequential lobing and conical scan compare echoes taken at different times, so a fluctuating target looks like angle motion. Monopulse does not.

quiz.q: Define boresight and state the value of the angle error signal there.
quiz.a: Boresight is the electrical axis of the antenna: the direction in which the angle error signal is zero. On a squinted or scanned feed it is the crossover or rotation axis, where the difference channel nulls.

quiz.q: Name the three channels a monopulse comparator forms from four squinted beams.
quiz.a: The sum channel Σ = A + B + C + D, the azimuth difference Δaz = (A + B) − (C + D), and the elevation difference Δel = (A + C) − (B + D).

quiz.q: Why is Δ/Σ used as the error signal rather than Δ alone?
quiz.a: Dividing by the sum normalises the reading. A strong echo and a weak echo from the same direction give different Δ but the same Δ/Σ, so the indicated angle no longer depends on range, radar cross section or transmitter power.

quiz.q: Why does conical scan manage with one receiver while amplitude-comparison monopulse needs three?
quiz.a: Conical scan puts the angle information on one beam sequentially in time, so one receiver sees everything. Monopulse needs all beams on the same pulse, so each difference channel needs its own matched receiver, or very fast switching between them.

quiz.q: A monopulse radar gives Σ = 8 V and Δ = 0.4 V, with error slope k = 2.0 per degree. Find Δ/Σ and the angle error.
quiz.a: Δ/Σ = 0.4/8 = 0.05. θ = 0.05/2.0 = 0.025°. The servo moves the antenna 0.025° to null the difference channel.

quiz.q: A target's radar cross section fluctuates strongly from pulse to pulse. Which of the three tracking schemes gives the largest angle error, and why?
quiz.a: Sequential lobing is worst, because the left and right beams are sampled on different pulses and a fading echo looks like an angle change. Conical scan also suffers, since fading at the scan rate is indistinguishable from an off-boresight target. Monopulse is unaffected because all channels come from the same pulse.

quiz.q: A jammer transmits a signal amplitude-modulated at the conical scan rate. Explain the effect on the tracker and say what defeats it.
quiz.a: The envelope detector cannot separate the false modulation from a genuine off-boresight target, so it produces a false angle error and the servo is pulled off target. Randomising the scan rate, or scanning only on receive (COSRO) with a stationary transmit beam, defeats a repeater jammer because the false modulation no longer matches the receiver scan. Monopulse, which measures angle within a single pulse, defeats it completely.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern trackers replace the four-horn cluster with a planar or active electronically scanned array, where sum and difference beams are formed digitally from many elements and several targets are tracked at once (track-while-scan). The same sum-difference idea appears in satellite ground stations and in missile seekers that must work from a single pulse. Glint and angle noise are still modelled statistically. Search terms: monopulse comparator, sum-difference beamforming, angle glint, track-while-scan.
